text:
Africa’s next industrial park may gain more from the pipe between two factories than from another stand-alone “green” technology.

Rwanda is making that choice now. The country has two special economic zones and eight industrial parks containing more than 320 factories, and in August announced Rwf10 billion for basic infrastructure in four priority parks. At the same time, it is studying how Korea organised industrial symbiosis: networks in which heat, water, energy and by-products move between firms instead of being treated as separate waste and input problems.

The commercial logic is strong. One plant can be rejecting heat while its neighbour burns fuel to create it. A food processor can pay to dispose of material another business could use. Several tenants can maintain separate treatment, logistics or backup-power systems because nobody has the mandate to organise a shared service.

But the implementation evidence matters more than the diagrams. UNIDO’s first Global Eco-Industrial Parks Programme phase identified 783 opportunities across 21 parks in seven countries. At the reporting cut-off, 177 had been implemented. The gap between an identified saving and an operating asset is the real story: volumes must match, quality must be dependable, regulation must permit the exchange, infrastructure must be financed, and firms must be willing to depend on one another.

StoneComms’ conclusion is that an eco-industrial park is not a landscaped estate with solar streetlights. It is a coordination institution backed by infrastructure, data and contracts.

We propose a six-gate Symbiosis Readiness Test:

Measure the resource baseline.
Match a credible source and user.
Clear the legal and safety rules.
Connect the shared backbone.
Operate it through an accountable park entity.
Finance the asset — and prove the savings.

The point is not to force complexity everywhere. In some parks, reliable power, wastewater treatment and professional management are still the higher priority. A shared heat network is not progress if the underlying cluster is commercially weak. The test is designed to show the difference before capital is committed.

For governments, park operators, development financiers and manufacturers, the strategic question is simple: are we financing “green features”, or shared production systems that can lower operating cost and strengthen competitiveness?
